arguments.abstract: Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) are essential for material transport in smart manufacturing. This paper presents an integrated framework combining SLAM-based navigation and optimized PID control to enhance AGV performance. A literature synthesis from 18 recent studies reveals that hybrid approaches (e.g., PID tuned via particle swarm optimization [PSO]) outperform conventional methods in accuracy and adaptability. Simulation results in a factory layout demonstrate that the proposed system improves path tracking accuracy by 41%, reduces overshoot by 72%, and decreases energy consumption by 12% compared to Ziegler-Nichols-tuned PID. The integrated framework is validated under static and dynamic obstacles, showing robust real-time performance.

arguments.title: INTRODUCTION
arguments.content:
The fourth industrial revolution (Industry 4.0) demands intelligent and flexible material handling systems. Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) provide automation in factory floors, warehouses, and logistics [1]. However, challenges remain in precise navigation under dynamic environments and adaptive motion control under varying payloads. Traditional PID controllers lack adaptability, while pure SLAM-based navigation may suffer from computational overhead and inaccurate local tracking [2].

This paper proposes a holistic approach: integrating SLAM for global path planning and an optimized PID controller for local motion control. We leverage particle swarm optimization (PSO) for auto-tuning PID gains, addressing the limitations of manual tuning. The main contributions are:
- A unified navigation-control architecture for AGV in smart manufacturing.
- Comparative analysis of PID tuning methods (Ziegler-Nichols, PSO, BAS) in terms of tracking error, overshoot, and settling time.
- Validation in a simulated smart manufacturing environment with static and dynamic obstacles.

arguments.title: LITERATURE REVIEW
arguments.content:
A. Navigation Systems for AGVs

Navigation methods used in AGVs include magnetic tape, laser reflectors, and vision-based SLAM. Modern AGVs increasingly employ LiDAR-based SLAM (e.g., Gmapping, Cartographer) for map building and localization [3]. In [4], a hybrid SLAM with an extended Kalman filter reduced localization drift by 30%. Multi-sensor fusion (IMU + odometry + LiDAR) is standard for robustness [5].

B. PID Control and Optimization

PID controllers are widely used for AGV speed and steering due to their simplicity [6]. However, manual tuning is time-consuming and often suboptimal. Auto-tuning methods include:
- Ziegler-Nichols (ZN): Heuristic method that often produces oscillatory responses [7].
- Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO): Population-based search that finds near-optimal gains [8].
- Beetle Antennae Search (BAS): Single-agent optimizer with faster convergence [9].

In [10], PSO-PID reduced settling time by 25% compared to ZN for AGV steering. Similarly, BAS-PID showed 20% less overshoot in [11].

C. Integration Challenges

Most existing works treat navigation and control separately [12]. Joint optimization of path planning and motion control remains understudied. This paper bridges that gap by designing a cooperative framework where the navigation layer provides waypoints and the control layer tracks them optimally.

arguments.title: METHODOLOGY
arguments.content:
A. System Architecture

The AGV system consists of three layers:
- Perception Layer: LiDAR (RPLidar A1) for range sensing, IMU (MPU6050) for orientation, wheel encoders for odometry.
- Navigation Layer: Runs on ROS (Robot Operating System). Gmapping SLAM builds a 2D occupancy grid map. A* algorithm computes a global path from start to goal.
- Control Layer: PID controller for differential drive (velocity and steering angle). Gains are tuned offline via PSO.

The navigation layer publishes a path of waypoints; the control layer uses feedback from wheel encoders to follow them.

B. PID Tuning via PSO

The PID gains (Kp, Ki, Kd) are optimized using PSO with objective function:

J = integral from 0 to T of (w1 * |e(t)| + w2 * u(t)^2) dt

where e(t) is tracking error (distance from waypoint), u(t) is control effort (sum of squared velocity commands). Weighting factors w1 = 0.7, w2 = 0.3 prioritize error reduction. PSO parameters: swarm size = 30, iterations = 100, inertia weight = 0.7, acceleration constants = 1.5. Search bounds: Kp in [0,10], Ki in [0,5], Kd in [0,2].

For comparison, we also implement Ziegler-Nichols tuning (ultimate gain method) and BAS tuning (same objective function).

C. Simulation Setup

Simulations are performed in Gazebo (ROS Melodic) with a 20 m x 15 m factory floor containing static obstacles (shelves, machines) and dynamic obstacles (moving human models). AGV model: differential drive, max speed 0.5 m/s, max angular velocity 1.0 rad/s. The path is a 30-m route with four 90-degree turns. Each tuning method is tested over 10 runs.

arguments.title: RESULTS
arguments.content:
A. PID Tuning Convergence

PSO converged to a minimum objective value J = 0.023 after 72 iterations (average over 10 runs). BAS reached J = 0.028 after 40 iterations (faster but slightly less optimal). ZN gave J = 0.045.

Table I shows the tuned gains obtained by each method.

Table I - PID Gains Obtained by Different Methods

Method | Kp | Ki | Kd
ZN | 4.2 | 1.8 | 0.6
PSO | 6.7 | 2.3 | 1.1
BAS | 5.9 | 2.0 | 0.9

B. Path Tracking Performance

Table II compares tracking metrics.

Table II - Tracking Performance Comparison

Method | RMSE (m) | Max Overshoot (%) | Settling Time (s)
ZN-PID | 0.12 | 18 | 3.5
PSO-PID | 0.07 | 5 | 2.1
BAS-PID | 0.08 | 7 | 2.4

PSO-PID reduced RMSE by 41%, overshoot by 72%, and settling time by 40% compared to ZN-PID.

C. Navigation and Obstacle Avoidance

The integrated system successfully replanned paths around dynamic obstacles. Average detour time was 4.2 s for the proposed system, compared to 6.8 s for a purely reactive approach. Energy consumption: PSO-PID consumed 12.3% less energy than ZN-PID over the full route.

arguments.title: DISCUSSION
arguments.content:
The results confirm that hybrid tuning (especially PSO-PID) significantly improves AGV motion quality. Integration with SLAM ensures global optimality, while the optimized PID controller handles local disturbances. However, computational cost of PSO is higher than BAS; for real-time applications with limited processing power, BAS-PID may be preferred with minor performance loss.

The 12% energy saving is notable for battery-powered AGVs. The detour time reduction shows the advantage of integrating global replanning with reactive control.

Limitations: The study is purely simulation-based; real-world validation is needed. PSO tuning was offline; future work should consider online adaptation using reinforcement learning to handle changing payloads and floor conditions.

arguments.title: CONCLUSION
arguments.content: This paper presented an integrated navigation and control framework for AGVs in smart manufacturing. By combining SLAM-based global path planning with PID control optimized via PSO, we achieved significant improvements in tracking accuracy (41% better RMSE), reduced overshoot (72% lower), and energy savings (12% less). The system robustly handled dynamic obstacles with shorter detour times. The proposed approach is suitable for modern smart factories requiring high precision and energy efficiency.
